HighLights
हरियाणा में वर्षा कम होने से गर्मी में वृद्धि हुई।
फरीदाबाद में वर्षा के बाद छज्जा गिरने से महिला की मौत।
आने वाले दिनों में तेज वर्षा का येलो अलर्ट जारी।
जागरण संवाददाता, हिसार। हरियाणा में मानसून के सक्रिय होने के बाद बुधवार को वर्षा कम हुई। प्रदेश में गर्मी बढ़ी और सिरसा का अधिकतम तापमान 38.2 डिग्री तक पहुंच गया। वहीं फरीदाबाद में वर्षा के बाद एक मकान के छज्जे पर पति-पत्नी खड़े थे।
अचानक से वह छज्जा गिर गया, जिससे महिला की मौत हो गई जबकि पति घायल हो गया। आने वाले दिनों में फिर से तेज वर्षा का यलो अलर्ट जारी किया गया है। भारत मौसम विज्ञान विभाग के अनुसार बुधवार को दिनभर धूप निकली रही।
इससे तापमान में तेजी से बढ़ोतरी हुई और सिरसा का तापमान 38 डिग्री पार कर गया। दोपहर बाद अचानक से एक बार मौसम में बदलाव हुआ लेकिन फिर से धूप निकलने के कारण उमस बढ़ गई। विज्ञानियों के अनुसार आने वाले दिनों में वर्षा का अलर्ट जारी किया गया है।
वर्षा के बाद भरभराकर गिरा जर्जर छज्जा
डबुआ थाना क्षेत्र की डबुआ कालोनी में वर्षा के बाद एक मकान का जर्जर छज्जा गिरने से छह माह की बच्ची की मां लाडली खातून (28) की मौत हो गई। वह बिहार के सारण जिले की रहने वाली थी और अपने पति कुसमा मोहम्मद व छह माह की बेटी के साथ डबुआ कालोनी की 27 फीट रोड स्थित गली नंबर चार में रमन भारद्वाज के मकान में किराये पर रहती थी।
खबरें और भी
परिवार करीब दो माह पहले ही रोजगार की तलाश में फरीदाबाद आया था। सुबह करीब 11 बजे वर्षा के बाद लाडली खातून और उनका पति मकान के छज्जे पर खड़े थे। लगातार वर्षा के कारण कमजोर हो चुका छज्जा अचानक भरभराकर गिर गया।
छज्जे के साथ महिला व उसका पति भी नीचे गिर गए। इसमें महिला मलबे के नीचे दबकर गंभीर रूप से घायल हो गई, जबकि पति को मामूली चोट लगी। तेज आवाज सुनकर आसपास के लोग मौके पर पहुंचे। लोगों ने मलबा हटाकर महिला को बाहर निकाला और तुरंत सिविल अस्पताल पहुंचाया, लेकिन गंभीर चोटों के कारण डाक्टर उन्हें बचा नहीं सके।

Every morning, Rekhaben and her husband push their vegetable cart onto the streets of Ahmedabad, India, knowing they will spend the day under the scorching sun. During the hottest hours, they take turns resting in the shade in a nearby park while the other watches over their cart, doing what they can to earn a living despite rising temperatures.
Extreme heat in 2025 left Rekhaben so weak that she needed days of medical treatment, including IV drips and injections. But staying home was not an option. Like millions of informal workers across South Asia, her family’s income depends on what she and her husband earn each day.
Rekhaben's story is becoming increasingly common across South Asia. The region needs to create jobs for about 280 million new working-age people by 2050. Cities will be at the center of this effort. Yet, as temperatures rise, extreme heat is emerging as one of the greatest threats to jobs, productivity, and economic growth.
A new World Bank report, A Livable Future: Tackling Extreme Heat for Jobs and Growth in South Asia's Cities, finds that increasing heat strains infrastructure, disrupts businesses, reduces jobs, and erodes productivity and incomes, particularly for those who can least afford it. Managing extreme heat is no longer just a climate imperative. It has become central to South Asia's jobs and growth agenda.
Unlike floods or storms, heat leaves few visible signs of destruction, yet its economic costs are enormous. The number of South Asians facing a month or more each year of dangerous heat stress - when the human body cannot maintain a safe temperature without active cooling - is projected to quadruple by 2070, from 120 million today to 520 million.
Much of the human cost does not appear in official statistics. Heat-related deaths are typically recorded as cardiac or renal failure, so a five-day heatwave associated with some 30,000 excess deaths can pass unrecorded as a heat event.
Yet extreme heat already subtracts the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs annually, as businesses face disruptions to power, transport, and operations and workers slow down, stop work, or become ill. The poor bear the greatest burden. A heatwave can cause informal workers to lose 40 percent of their earnings while also raising costs for water, cooling, and healthcare. Without adaptation, rising temperatures could reduce South Asia's GDP by nearly 7 percent by 2050 - the steepest projected loss of any developing region - reducing investment, government revenues, and long-term competitiveness.

Extreme heat is costing South Asia nearly the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs every year and is on track to diminish the region's economy by nearly 7% by 2050, according to a new World Bank report published yesterday (29 July).
It also states that by 2070, around 520 million people across South Asia could experience at least one month of dangerous heat each year, four times as many as today.
The report was prepared with support from the Resilient Asia Program (RAP), funded by the UK Government's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) through its flagship Climate Action for a Resilient Asia (CARA) programme.
The World Bank's Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery (GFDRR) and the City Resilience Program (CRP) also supported the preparation of the report.
Extreme heat is also putting growing pressure on health systems and critical infrastructure, while hitting low-income households, informal workers, women, the elderly, and children the hardest.
The report argues that heat should no longer be treated as a seasonal emergency. Instead, it should become a core development priority that is integrated into urban planning, infrastructure investment, public policy, and private sector development.
"South Asia's cities are central to the region's future, but rising temperatures are putting jobs, livelihoods, and economic growth at risk," said Johannes Zutt, World Bank vice president for South Asia.
"Building heat- resilient cities is not only about protecting people from rising temperatures. It is about safeguarding jobs, boosting productivity, attracting investment, and ensuring cities continue to drive economic growth. By acting now, countries can build more resilient, competitive, and livable cities that create opportunities for future generations," he added.
The report provides policymakers with a practical roadmap that can be implemented through existing institutions and financing mechanisms.
It recommends investing in heat-resilient infrastructure, strengthening Heat Action Plans, protecting vulnerable workers, expanding sustainable cooling, improving early warning systems, and mobilising public and private investment to build more resilient cities.
"Across South Asia, extreme heat is destroying livelihoods, impacting public health, depressing productivity, and pushing the most vulnerable further into poverty," said John Warburton, Climate Resilience lead for Asia Pacific at the UK's Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office.
"This is a development crisis that calls for sustained action across sectors. That is why the UK government, through our flagship Climate Action for a Resilient Asia programme, is committed to working with the World Bank and other partners to build knowledge, inform policies, and unlock the investment needs in the region to adapt to a warming planet," Warburton added.
The report further said that many of the solutions already exist as cities across South Asia are showing how Heat Action Plans, resilient infrastructure, urban greening, early warning systems, and efficient cooling can save lives, protect workers, and reduce economic losses.
Scaling these approaches will require stronger institutions, better coordination, and greater public and private investment, said the report.
It further recommended that investing in heat resilience is essential to protect people, strengthen economies, and secure the region's long-term prosperity.

Japan earthquake death toll rises to 34 as evacuees battle sweltering heat
The number of people who have died after a powerful earthquake hit southwestern Japan has risen to 34, authorities in Kumamoto prefecture said on Thursday.
Rescuers are still working to find survivors after the magnitude 6.8 earthquake hit Kumamoto prefecture on Kyushu island on Tuesday, causing widespread damage to houses and power lines.
Several people died after part of a shopping centre collapsed and an explosion ripped through the mall about an hour later.
Thousands of displaced residents are now staying in evacuation centres - though the challenge is to keep them cool and hydrated as the region battles sweltering heat.
Temperatures could reach 39C in the prefecture in the coming days, according to forecasts, with officials urging survivors and rescuers to take precautions against heatstroke.
On Wednesday, Japan's defence minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced the delivery of 300 air conditioners to Kumamoto, with 150 of the units bound for evacuation centres.
Around 9,000 displaced residents have been put up in evacuation centres, and more than 30,000 households were out of power as of Wednesday.
Yukiya Sanoue, who works at one of the centres, told the BBC that heat stroke was the biggest concern at his facility, which hosts about 1,000 people. About 30% of the people at his evacuation centre are senior citizens.
He said their electricity and water supplies had stopped since the earthquake, and the centre had been without air conditioning until Wednesday afternoon when they received a generator.
Quite a few people are suffering from conditions similar to heatstroke, and several have been taken to hospital, he said.
More than 100 aftershocks have been recorded since the initial quake, and many have taken to sleeping in their cars for fear of further tremors.
Thousands of personnel have been deployed for search-and-rescue operations. Many are digging through rubble at Kashima's Aeon shopping centre, one of the worst-hit buildings where a portion of the second floor collapsed.
The mall was also rocked by an explosion about an hour after the initial quake.
The president of Aeon said it was "very likely" a gas explosion, though the cause of the blast remains under investigation.
A cat cafe inside the mall said on Wednesday that its 25 cats, which had been left behind during the chaos of the quake, had all since been safely rescued.
The quake-hit Aeon mall in Kumamoto had just reopened last month as a revamped shopping complex. It had previously been damaged during a series of strong earthquakes in April 2016, which killed 278 people in the region.
Rescuers were also combing a Nippon Paper factory in Yatsushiro city, where at least five people have died after the factory partially collapsed during the quake.

A heat wave is expected to reach Israel beginning on Friday, peaking on Saturday and Sunday. It will be accompanied by dry conditions and strong winds in northern Israel, raising the risk of wildfires.
The hottest area is expected to be around the Sea of Galilee and the northern valleys, where temperatures could climb to as high as 47C on Sunday. Israel Meteorological Service Director Dr. Amir Givati stated that if this occurs, it would break the regional temperature record set about 30 years ago, when 46.8C was recorded at Beit Tsaida on August 9, 1998.
On Thursday, temperatures will rise slightly, and conditions will be hotter than usual, with heat wave conditions in the hills and inland areas, while the Coastal Plain will remain hot and humid. Heavy to extreme heat is expected across most of the country.

Heavy heat is expected in the northern Golan Heights, the western Galilee, the Carmel region, Ramat Menashe, the Coastal Plain, the Shephelah, the central hills, the northern Negev, and the Negev Highlands.

On Saturday, temperatures will remain hotter than usual, with heat wave conditions in the hills and inland areas, while humid conditions continue along the Coastal Plain. The heat will intensify further, with heavy to extreme conditions expected nationwide.
On Sunday, the weather will remain hotter than usual, with heat wave conditions in the hills and inland areas, and continued humidity along the Coastal Plain. Heavy to extreme heat will continue throughout the country.

Iced matcha lattes and a bigger range of salads and chicken rolls helped Greggs to boost its sales during the string of summer heatwaves, as the bakery said it was adapting to the UK’s increasingly hot summers.
Total sales at Britain’s biggest fast food business rose to £1.1bn for the first six months of the year, 7.2% higher than the same period a year earlier.
The rise in sales was largely down to extra stores, as the chain opened 34 new sites on a net basis, taking the total number of Greggs outlets across the country to 2,773 by the end of June.
The Newcastle-headquartered company said this year’s new shops had been performing well so far, which it attributed to its “disciplined focus on high-quality locations”.
Sales at the company’s existing stores rose by 2.1% between January and June, helped by a wave of price rises on key items at the start of 2026.
Roisin Currie, the chief executive, said Greggs did not expect to put up prices further this year as its prediction for cost inflation had taken a step back to 2% from 3%.
She said the company had been able to hedge 90% of its energy costs for this year and half of those for next year, protecting it from the recent surge in the oil price, while the cost of key commodities such as cocoa and coffee had stepped back after a period of high inflation.
The chain’s pre-tax profit rose by almost 20% from a year earlier to £76m for the first half of the year, which it said was because of cost control as well as growth in its “bake at home” range of frozen treats, which launched in Tesco earlier this year, while it expanded the range sold in Iceland supermarkets.
The results mark a turnaround compared with last summer when its sales and profits were hit as customers shunned pastries such as steak bakes and vegan sausage rolls during periods of hot weather.
That prompted analysts and consumers to ask whether the UK had hit “peak Greggs”, with Currie insisting otherwise last summer, saying the company had previously bounced back from other downturns.
That revival appears to be well under way, with Greggs saying the introduction of new products on its menus had helped attract health-conscious customers, even during the heatwaves.
A new chicken roll launched in April was hailed as a “standout success”, while Greggs said a relaunched salad range featuring more protein, including a chicken caesar salad and prawn layered pasta salad, had helped it offer healthier lunchtime options.
Currie said Greggs had adapted to the rise in the number of hot spells in the UK by introducing iced drinks to its range last year and a “more compelling” range of salads this year. “We have become more resilient as we have seen hot weather become more of a normality at certain points in the UK,” she said.
Greggs has also been able to appeal to new and younger customers by offering new drinks including lemonades, refreshers and matcha, the antioxidant-rich green tea that has become popular with gen Z consumers, defined as those born between 1997 and 2012.
Currie said the latest results showed the company “continued to outperform the market” and it still had room for more outlets, particularly in travel hubs, industrial sites, retail parks and by motorways.
She said: “We remain focused on opening shops in more catchments and introducing convenient ways for customers to pick up Greggs favourites, while broadening and innovating our menu in line with changing tastes and trends.”
Julie Palmer, a managing partner at the financial and real estate advisory group BTG, said Greggs was undeterred from store expansion plans despite the challenging economic outlook and growing use of weight-loss drugs.
“As any price rises can quickly translate into demand crumbling away, Greggs will have to continue walking the tightrope of pricing and controlling costs to retain and grow market share as the food-to-go provider of choice,” she said.

Extreme heat is costing South Asia the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs every year, while the region's economy could shrink by around 7 percent by 2050 if current trends continue, according to a new World Bank report.
The report, titled "A Livable Future: Protecting Jobs and Growth from Extreme Heat in South Asia's Cities," warns that rising temperatures are emerging as one of the biggest threats to employment, productivity and long-term economic growth across the region.
According to the report, by 2070, nearly 520 million people in South Asia could face dangerously high temperatures for at least one month each year—four times the current number.
The World Bank said South Asia is expected to add 280 million working-age people by 2050, but intensifying heat could undermine employment opportunities and economic expansion if adequate adaptation measures are not taken.
The report found that extreme heat is already reducing labour productivity, disrupting businesses and weakening the competitiveness of South Asian cities. It is also placing mounting pressure on healthcare systems and critical infrastructure, with low-income households, informal workers, women, children and the elderly bearing the greatest burden.
World Bank Vice President for South Asia Johannes Zutt said the region's cities are central to its future, but rising temperatures are putting jobs, livelihoods and economic growth at risk.
"Building heat-resilient cities is not only about protecting people from rising temperatures—it is about safeguarding jobs, boosting productivity, attracting investment and ensuring cities remain engines of economic growth," he said.
The report argues that extreme heat should no longer be treated as a seasonal hazard but as a core development challenge requiring integration into urban planning, infrastructure investment, public policy and private-sector development.
It outlines a roadmap for policymakers, recommending greater investment in heat-resilient infrastructure, stronger heat action plans, improved protection for vulnerable workers, expansion of sustainable cooling systems, enhanced early warning mechanisms and increased public-private investment.
John Warburton, Climate Resilience Lead for Asia-Pacific at the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), described extreme heat as a growing development crisis that is destroying livelihoods, harming public health, reducing productivity and pushing vulnerable communities deeper into poverty.
The report notes that practical solutions are already being implemented across parts of South Asia, including heat action plans, climate-resilient infrastructure, urban greening, early warning systems and efficient cooling technologies. However, scaling up these initiatives will require stronger institutions, better coordination and increased investment.
The World Bank cautioned that as urbanisation accelerates, the decisions governments make today will determine whether South Asia's cities continue to drive employment, innovation and economic growth—or become increasingly constrained by the escalating impacts of extreme heat.
The report was prepared under the Resilient Asia Program, funded by the UK's FCDO through its Climate Action for a Resilient Asia initiative, with additional support from the World Bank's Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery (GFDRR) and the City Resilience Programme.

Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for parts of UK on Thursday into the weekend, as a cold front moves into the UK.
However, with more than half of England and parts of Wales officially in drought, the coming days are unlikely to bring any rain to the driest areas of the country.
The latest UK heatwave peaked on Wednesday with temperatures soaring to 35.2C at Writtle in Essex. It was the hottest day for more than two weeks, when 35.2C was also recorded in Cotton in the Elms, Derbyshire, on 10 July.
It did not reach the highs experienced last month, when a new UK June temperature record of 38C was set at Lingwood in Norfolk on the 26th, which was also the hottest day of the year so far.
Last month's record was provisionally reported as 37.7C but the Met Office announced on Wednesday a new figure of 38.0C following a verification process.
It comes after drought was declared across more than half of England on Wednesday as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.
The Environment Agency (EA) announcement covered much of central, eastern and southern England, and was a public sign that further restrictions on water use might follow.
It added that the impacts are already being felt, including low river flows, early harvests and high risk of wildfires. More than 20 million people are already under hosepipe bans.
North Wales and the Upper Severn river basin entered drought conditions last week, Natural Resources Wales said.
Scotland does not declare drought but monitors "water scarcity". Some parts of eastern Scotland are in the most extreme category of "significant scarcity", according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.
Northern Ireland is not currently in drought.
Is the heatwave over?
Three consecutive days meeting the threshold temperature are required for it to be considered a heatwave.
The extent of this latest heatwave has been limited because Monday did not reach the threshold across most of the Midlands, East Anglia and central southern England.
Tuesday and Wednesday were both hot days, but the cold front moving in on Thursday drops the temperatures just below the threshold for many, meaning many areas narrowly miss the mark.
However, the cold front does not quite reach East Anglia and south-east England, so the heat hangs on for one more day with temperatures reaching the high 20s or possibly 30C in the hottest areas, which will therefore reach three days above the threshold.
For Friday and the weekend, temperatures in central and eastern England will still reach the mid-20s so it will still feel warm in the sunshine.
Sunday will probably turn a bit warmer again with temperatures into the high 20s. The weather will be cool in the north-west of the UK with temperatures often below average.
Is there any rain on the way?
For the most parched areas of the UK, there is unlikely to be any rain over the next few days.
Wisley in Surrey has had 42 consecutive dry days as of Tuesday 29 July. The weakening cold front should reach Wisley but is unlikely to produce any rain there.
The wettest weather will affect the north-west of the UK, which has already seen plenty of rain this month. Aultbea in the Highlands has already had about a third more rain than its July average.
Next week there is going to be more rain in the forecast, and again the north-west will probably end up being the wettest area.
A few forecast models produce some useful rain in the south too but this is far less certain with many models producing little if any rain. It is too soon to know for sure.
The summer so far has seen temperature records tumble.
We have now had seven days with temperatures over 35C, beating the previous record of five set in 1976 and equalled in 2020.
There have been 31 days with temperatures over 30C, not far off the record of 34 days set in 1995 and comfortably beating 1976, which had 24 days.
There is still plenty of time left this summer to equal or beat this mark.

Heat waves intensify as climate changes. These tips can help.
As heat waves become more frequent and intense due to climate change, finding ways to stay cool beyond simply turning up the air conditioning can be challenging, but not impossible.
Extreme heat is a prolonged period of high heat and humidity with temperatures substantially above normal for a specific location and time of year, typically lasting two or more days, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
Here are 11 ways to beat the heat this summer, based on guidance from organizations including the World Health Organization:
Turning libraries, malls and movie theaters
Instead of staying home in overheated apartments, consider visiting an air-conditioned public space such as libraries, shopping centers, museums, and theaters. Using cooling centers or other air-conditioned buildings when home cooling is inadequate is also an option.
Creating DIY "Cool Rooms" at home
Rather than cooling an entire house, homeowners are concentrating cooling efforts in one room. Closing blinds, sealing gaps around windows, blocking sunlight, and using a single air-conditioned room during the hottest part of the day is an option. Consider shading windows and keeping homes closed during peak heat.
Use cooler nighttime air
Many residents open windows overnight and early in the morning to bring cooler air indoors, then close windows and curtains after sunrise to trap it inside. Use cooler nighttime air to reduce indoor heat buildup.
Wear wet clothing or cooling towels
People increasingly use damp bandanas, cooling towels, misting bottles and lightly wetted clothing to stay cool.
Organize heat buddy networks
Communities are creating informal systems to check on seniors, people with disabilities and people living alone. These routine wellness checks during heat emergencies are helpful.
Shift daily schedules
Construction workers, runners, gardeners, dog owners and commuters are moving activities to dawn, evening or nighttime hours. Avoiding strenuous activity during the hottest part of the day is key.
Install reflective cool-roof coatings
Some homeowners are painting roofs with reflective white or light-colored coatings. Cool roofs absorb less solar heat and can lower indoor temperatures while reducing cooling costs.
Grow shade with canopies and plants
People are installing shade sails, pergolas, trellises, climbing vines and container gardens to create cooler microclimates around homes and patios. Heat-island experts identify shade and vegetation as key strategies for reducing local temperatures.
Use splash pads and public pools
Families are treating municipal pools, splash pads and water parks as essential heat-relief resources rather than purely recreational amenities. Georgia communities actively promote public pools and splash pads during heat advisories.
Use community cooling hubs
Neighborhood groups, churches and nonprofits are transforming community buildings into temporary cooling hubs that provide water, shade, charging stations and health information. Community cooling centers are an effective heat-protection strategy.
Replace pavement with cooler surfaces
Homeowners and neighborhood groups are removing unnecessary asphalt, adding vegetation, using lighter-colored materials and creating permeable landscaping. Urban climate experts identify these approaches as effective ways to combat urban heat islands.
CDC tips for staying cool outdoors
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends:
- Do outdoor activities during the coolest parts of the day or evening, if possible.
- Carry a water bottle.
- Drink water and refill your bottle throughout the day.
- Consider limiting beverages high in sugar and sodium, as well as caffeine and alcohol.

Mandy Bourne lives with her 80‑year‑old mum in a top‑floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves.
For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains.
Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged‑up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool.
Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in."
That retained warmth can push night‑time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths.
Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder".
Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised.
"We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes.
Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices.
As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon?
Historic choices
For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus.
Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance.
In 2023, $1.8trn was given to mitigation, whilst adaptation did not secure even 5% of that – it scraped $65bn globally.
Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged.
In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world.
Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it.
The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other.
Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax.
Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering.
The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat – but how much to spend on each.
Profit wins out
There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus – it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term.
Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law.
Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year.
Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans.
"Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good."
Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets.
"We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050."
"We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference."
One of the most controversial ideas in the report is on air conditioning. Right now, only 5% or so of English homes have a cooling unit. The Committee recommends fitting these devices in hospitals and care homes within 10 years, and schools in 25 years.
This goes against years of government advice that passive cooling was the preferred method - using shade, ventilation and other design features to bring down temperatures, not mechanical means.
Prof Mat Santamouris from the University of New South Wales, is the world's most-cited researcher on urban overheating.
Machines, he argues, should be the last line of defence: reflective roofing alone, in one of his studies, dragged indoor temperatures from around 43C towards 30C, while a ceiling fan gives comfort for a fraction of the cost.
Putting up unshaded glass towers in cities, he says, is "crazy". "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change."
Santamouris is scathing about who is driving the air con demand - the industry, he says, is "extremely powerful" – adding that passive cooling adds its own economic growth, as money is spent on plumbers and builders.
Against him stand those who think Britain's hostility to cooling has curdled into a type of masochism.
David Lawrence, of the Centre for British Progress think tank, puts it plainly: we don't tell people to insulate their homes in winter and then skip the radiators. So why insist shade and shutters are enough in summer?
He points out that air conditioning is standard now in offices, hotels and shops, "but we don't expect it for schools and hospitals - which is kind of odd, because those are places where millions of people are every day", and where heat measurably dents concentration, learning and health.
This dispute over the pros and cons of the technology is becoming political.
Some London councils, following a planning "cooling hierarchy", say low‑energy ways of keeping homes cool should be prioritised over air conditioning and in a small number of cases have ordered property owners to remove them; the Conservative front bench calls it "dark ages" miserabilism; other MPs and political commentators demand an "air-con revolution".
Since April, in England and Wales the Boiler Upgrade Scheme has offered £2,500 towards a reversible air-air heat pump: a machine that warms a home in winter and cools it in summer. It is, in all but name, Britain's first air-conditioning subsidy - but it is badged as a heat pump, and only worth a third of the £7,500 for a heating-only model.
Such has been the silence around this grant, that in its first month only around 45 households claimed it. By comparison, the numbers claiming a heating-only model ran into the thousands.
In Scotland homeowners can also get a £7,500 grant for a heat pump via its Home Energy scheme - but for air-air versions that could offer cooling there is no funding at all. And in Northern Ireland there is no universal heat pump grant offered for households.
Under the terms of the England and Wales scheme, some people cannot apply at all. It is closed to social housing and newbuilds - which many argue shuts out the very people most exposed.
Take Woolwich, in south-east London, where a resident called Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave.
She calls the building "inhumane"; she and around twenty neighbours in Canada Court and Clifton Lodge are taking their landlord, the housing association PA Housing, to court over homes they say are unfit to live in.
Even the landlord half-concedes the ground: its chief executive accepts that a growing number of residents face "uncomfortably warm temperatures … due to the changing climate", in homes "designed to keep heat in rather than keep them cool".
Keisha is exactly the tenant the state's new cooling grant might have been written for. But as a social tenant, she is barred from it.
Baroness Brown's committee finds the most deprived neighbourhoods are more than seven times as likely to be badly exposed to heat.
The government had a long-running scheme for supporting upgrades to social housing - ECO - but it will close after this year over reports of "cowboy" installations. The replacement scheme, if it continues under the new government, will not start until next year.
Demand for air-con
There is a cruel physics beneath the financial unfairness.
Air conditioning doesn't destroy heat, it moves it - out of the flat and into the street, where, Santamouris says, it warms the air your neighbours breathe and drives up the demand for still more cooling, by about a third in his studies of Sydney.
The machines keeping the financially comfortable cool make everyone else's nights worse; and as wealthier households cool their rooms, the rest fall further behind. A thermal divide, opening street by street.
And it lands on the electricity grid at the worst possible moment.
The electricity demand for cooling peaks on still, hot evenings - just as the wind drops and solar fades, leaving gas to supply the extra energy. In so doing, further greenhouse gas emissions are generated, adding bit by bit to the climate change effect – the very one driving the temperatures and the demand for air conditioning.
And the same heat that drives the demand also weakens the supply: gas turbines lose output as the air warms, and in June several UK plants had to be turned down.
But such is the scale of the heat that people are voting with their wallets - demand for portable air con units is through the roof, regardless of grants and the environment.
The evidence from experts is that we should not go down this road.
Santamouris and Baroness Brown reach for the same answer: passive cooling first, machines where genuinely needed, clean power behind them, and the lesson that France learned painfully in the deadly heatwave of 2003 - the vulnerable protected rather than left to improvise.
Cooling every home by machine would strain the grid and warm the streets, hampering the effort to slow the warming that drives the demand.
In Tokyo, Santamouris says, so many air conditioners now pump their waste heat into the air that the exhaust alone generates heat that's measured at close to a thousand watts of warming on every square metre - as much energy as falls from the sky at midday. "It's another sun," he adds with emphasis, "another sun."
"It's not the same in London. But if we continue in the same way, in some years we will have the same results."
The heat of this year and last, and the prospects of it being repeated, is a future Jo Shields is upset by.
"It's our survival," she says. Most days, she tries to bury the thought of it - "because otherwise it terrifies me."
Meanwhile Mandy says she is grateful that the new community room with its air conditioning is providing some immediate respite for her and her mum.
"We sit there all day with it on, it helps so much I want one in my flat."

FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- Central Californians are having to wake up earlier to get in their exercise.
"We usually play a couple of hours... and we're done for the day. It's too hot, and so, we're pretty much inside after that," said Sherry Ogden, a pickleball player.
Fresno has had low triple digits for the last few weeks.
But now it's going to get hotter.
As Action News has been warning you about the impending high heat, paramedics are already hard at work.
"Summertime is busy. You know, temperatures rise, and calls increase," said Jessica Bernal, the Basic Life Support Operation Manager for American Ambulance in Fresno.
American Ambulance says every Summer, it responds to numerous heat-related illness calls -- mainly, heat exhaustion and heat stroke.
"They're sweating, they're feeling fatigue, nausea, vomiting -- that's heat exhaustion. Then, when we talk about heat strokes, we're looking for someone who is not sweating. Someone that is confused or altered, not acting like themselves," said Bernal.
"You do the best you can. You get some exercise, even though it's so hot. Stay cool, drink lots of water," said Ogden.
Bernal also says it's important to wear sunscreen and to reapply it regularly.
"Make sure that you protect your skin so you can prevent any type of burns," said Bernal. "It could be painful, really uncomfortable. If that ever occurs, we advise you to go ahead and go to urgent care or the ER to go ahead and seek treatment."
Paramedics also recommend wearing long sleeves, staying in the shade, and keeping an eye on others -- especially high-risk groups like children and seniors.
The hot weather can also cause heart problems.
As the heart works harder to cool the body, it can create severe strain that can trigger dehydration, low blood pressure, and heart attacks.

Prices of locally grown aromatic rice have surged to an all-time high of Tk 220-230 per kg at the retail level, causing extra burden on consumers.
Traders and market analysts attributed the sharp price hike to persistent export of fragrant rice coupled with its supply shortage in the local market.
The Trading Corporation of Bangladesh (TCB) recorded a 50-per cent rise in the prices of aromatic rice over the past four months, while market sources said the retail price of the same shot up by Tk 65-80 per kg during the period.
Local varieties of aromatic l rice, including Chinigura and Kalijeera, are currently selling at Tk 190-230 per kg in the market.
Branded packaged aromatic rice is being sold at around Tk 190 per kg, up from Tk 170 two weeks ago and Tk 150-160 four months earlier.
Loose Chinigura variety of rice is now retailing at Tk 220-230 per kg compared to Tk180-190 a couple of weeks ago and Tk 135-140 per kg in February.
Alif Islam, a grocer at Buddhijibir Dhal in Mohammadpur area, said the prices of aromatic rice began rising in February after the government announced that private-sector would be allowed to export the same.
He said the interim government permitted its exports just ahead of the holy month of Ramadan, triggering a steady rise in domestic prices of the item.
The interim government first lifted a nearly two-year export ban in April 2025, allowing 133 companies to export 25,000 tonnes of aromatic rice.
In February 2026, the Ministry of Commerce again allowed its exports.
In May this year, the ministry authorised 211 companies to export 36,520 tonnes of aromatic rice until December 31, subject to nine conditions.
Sazzad Ali, a rice trader at Mohammadpur Krishi Market, said some large companies dominate both the domestic and export markets for aromatic rice.
He estimated that seven to eight companies now control 60-70 per cent of the aromatic rice market.
"They are the major exporters as well as the leading players in the domestic market," he said, adding that there is currently a shortage of aromatic rice in the market.
When asked, Mohammad Ishakul Hossain, president of the Bangladesh Rice Exporters Association, said about 2,000-2100 tonnes of shipment could be made in the last one month.
He said it is a tiny amount compared to the production of above 1.0 million tonnes.
He said big millers have a stockpile and they are using the export announcement as a way to make huge profits. Shamsul Alam, a miller at Nilphamari, said auto rice millers can hardly store aromatic rice.
He said only a small number of automated mill owners do businesses of aromatic rice throughout the year.
Allowing export of aromatic incentivised the market, he added.
Anowar Hossain Babul, proprietor of Olima Traders in Nilphamari, said half of the aromatic rice is being turned into finer 'parboiled rice' at the beginning of the season. Rising consumption of aromatic rice has also resulted in a supply shortage for the produce.
Agricultural economist Prof Golam Hafeez Kennedy said the country experienced crop losses during the Boro season, while Aus output also declined to some extent.
He said global aromatic rice prices have been rising steadily in recent months also. "This is not an ideal time for Bangladesh to export such a large volume of rice," he said.
Humayun Kabir Bhuiyan, Secretary of the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), said it is unfair for local consumers.
"The problem lies in oligopoly. A few dominant business groups continue to control both the domestic and export markets," he said.
He urged the government to immediately suspend aromatic rice exports to safeguard the country's food security.
According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), Bangladesh produces more than 40 million tonnes of rice annually, of which aromatic rice accounts for around 1.2-1.5 million tonnes.
The country's annual demand for aromatic rice is 0.7-0.8 million tonnes.

ALDEA DEL FRESNO, Spain: Thousands who fled huge wildfires in Spain returned home on Wednesday while in France firefighters battled raging flames as a new heatwave gripped the region.
The neighboring countries have been gripped by some of the worst forest fires in living memory over the past week, burning vast areas and forcing tens of thousands from their homes.
Spain lifted remaining evacuation orders for Avila province and for the last two towns near Madrid that had been evacuated on Wednesday. While some evacuees returned to untouched homes, others found only devastation.
“I’m happy — I couldn’t wait to come home and have my coffee and breakfast,” said Maria Jesus Perez Blanca, in her seventies. She was one of about a dozen returnees at the cafes of Aldea del Fresno, west of Madrid on Wednesday morning.
But 12 kilometers (eight miles) away in Pelayos de la Presa, David Rodriguez was knocking down the scorched remains of his home.
“It’s a disaster. Just look at it,” he said. “All my memories, everything I had was here. My dad built it 40 years ago and everything has been lost.”
Officials said on Wednesday that better overnight conditions had helped crews stabilize the fire area, and Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the coming hours would be “decisive” in the battle to extinguish all the remaining flames.
In France, the Gironde region reported a second calm night and said the massive fire west of France’s wine-making capital of Bordeaux remained stable despite a spike in temperatures on Wednesday as the fourth heatwave of the summer roasted the area.
“If the night goes well, we can reasonably be more optimistic for tomorrow and the days to come,” Sophie Brocas, a senior regional official, said.
In the southeastern region of Var, however, more than 600 people were forced to flee after a fresh fire erupted in the region nestled along France’s Mediterranean coast between the cities of Marseille and Nice.
The new fire erupted less than a day after another blaze in the Var was brought under control.
Another forest fire erupted in the eastern region of Burgundy near the city of Dijon, sweeping across 125 hectares but without causing any casualties or damage to homes, local officials said.
It began in the afternoon in the Combe du Vaulon, a dry valley located in the wine-growing commune of Couchey, about 10 kilometers (six miles) southwest of Dijon.
Europe-wide disaster
Europe has been gripped by successive heatwaves and a major drought this year, which scientists have attributed to human-caused climate change.
Extreme heat has parched vegetation that grew vigorously during wet weather earlier in the year, creating tinderbox conditions.
In Spain, 207,000 hectares (511,000 acres) of land has burned nationwide, among the largest areas in any January to July period on record according to the European Forest Fire Information System. Spanish authorities have reported marginally different figures.
In France, some 92,000 hectares have burned over the same period — the largest area ever documented in records that date back two decades.
While the current focus is on Western Europe, the EU warned this week that fire-prone conditions would spread toward the center of the continent in the coming days.
Emergency crews were already tackling a blaze on the Greek island of Paros. Two firefighters died fighting fires in Crete and a third near the Peloponnese port of Gytheio.
Fires in Turkiye have already forced the evacuation of hundreds of people around tourist beaches in the south, with hundreds of firefighters tackling the flames.
